world_behind.title: The wilderness child
world_behind.text: Jacob was born on the trail (1 Ne. 18:7), grieved on the ship for his mother (18:19), and grew up inside the family quarrel. The blessing opens by naming that history, "thou hast suffered afflictions and much sorrow, because of the rudeness of thy brethren" (v. 1), with the same word the record used for the shipboard revelry that started it. The chapter's high doctrine is aimed at one bruised boy.

world_behind.title: A second firstborn
world_behind.text: "My firstborn in the days of my tribulation" (v. 1) is careful legal language: Laman remains firstborn of the house, Jacob is firstborn of the exile. The family's structure now has two lines of precedence, one of birth and one of the covenant journey, and the record will follow the second.

world_behind.title: Grace and truth, before John
world_behind.text: "Full of grace and truth" (v. 6) is the phrase John's prologue will fix to the Word made flesh; its ancestry runs to Sinai, where the Lord self-describes as abundant in goodness and truth (Ex. 34:6). Lehi's Messiah carries the covenant God's own attribute pair.

world_behind.title: The preacher cites his sources
world_behind.text: "According to the things which I have read" (v. 17), "according to that which is written" (v. 17): Lehi's account of the fallen angel is presented as a reading of the brass plates, and Isaiah's taunt over the fallen day-star (Isa. 14:12) is the surviving text that best matches his reading.

world_behind.title: Two trees, by design
world_behind.text: Eden as Lehi tells it is a built environment for choice: "the forbidden fruit in opposition to the tree of life; the one being sweet and the other bitter" (v. 15). The garden's furniture embodies the opposition doctrine; the first commandment came with its alternative planted a short walk away.

world_behind.title: An unnamed prophet's good part
world_behind.text: "I have chosen the good part, according to the words of the prophet" (v. 30): the phrase matches the Lord's words at Bethany (Luke 10:42), centuries unwritten. Which prophet Lehi quotes is nowhere said; the record leaves the citation open, one more glimpse of a brass-plates library larger than ours.

cites.quote: I have chosen the good part, according to the words of the prophet

spans.text: I have chosen the good part, according to the words of the prophet

words.text: A fastening word, and a legal one: a punishment is affixed to a law the way a seal is affixed to a document, so the two cannot travel separately. Lehi fastens happiness the same way in the same breath, "which punishment that is affixed is in opposition to that of the happiness which is affixed" (v. 10). Consequence here is attached in advance, at both ends. Alma will pick the word up for his own long argument about justice and mercy, where the punishment stands "affixed opposite to the plan of happiness" (Alma 42:16).

cites.quote: which punishment that is affixed is in opposition to that of the happiness which is affixed

spans.text: which punishment that is affixed is in opposition to that of the happiness which is affixed

words.text: "All things must needs be a compound in one" (v. 11): the argument's technical term for reality without contraries, a mixture so total nothing stands distinct from anything. Such a world, Lehi reasons, "must needs remain as dead" (v. 11): no difference, no motion, no purpose. The word gives the opposition doctrine its precise alternative, and it is oblivion.

cites.quote: All things must needs be a compound in one

spans.text: All things must needs be a compound in one

words.text: The state of feeling nothing at all. The word appears once in this record and never in the King James Bible. Lehi needs a name for what is left when every opposite has been folded together, and verse 11 supplies it at the end of the list: righteousness, wickedness, holiness, misery, good, bad, and then nothing that can register any of them. The argument required a word for total absence, and the record spends one here.

"Man could not act for himself save it should be that he was enticed by the one or the other" (v. 16): agency's strangest requirement. Freedom is not the absence of pulls but the presence of both; a soul drawn only one way is not choosing. The verse quietly dignifies temptation's existence as a condition of moral life, without excusing the tempter.

words.text: The testing-time word from the vision cycle (1 Ne. 10:21) returns with its mechanism: days "prolonged" (v. 21), time "lengthened" (v. 21), so "that they might repent while in the flesh" (v. 21). Lehi then dates himself by his own doctrine, speaking "in the last days of my probation" (v. 30): the teacher inside the test he is describing.

words.text: Nothing charming about it. To captivate is to take captive, and the verse means the older sense flatly: choosing by the will of the flesh gives the devil "power to captivate, to bring you down to hell" (v. 29). Two verses earlier the alternatives were liberty and captivity, so the closing warning is about ownership. Alma keeps the word in its hard sense when he sets "the power and captivation of the devil" (Alma 9:28) opposite the deliverance of Christ.

phrases.term: He shall consecrate thine afflictions for thy gain
phrases.text: The blessing's thesis, delivered before any theology. Yesterday the verb was for land (2 Ne. 1:7, 32); today it is for wounds: to consecrate is to seize for sacred use, so what the brothers' rudeness cost Jacob will be employed for his gain. The whole chapter then explains the machinery of such conversions: a Redeemer who turns a fall into the door of joy can turn a childhood's sorrow into gain.

Law in Lehi's argument has purposes, not just penalties, and only a sacrifice "unto all those who have a broken heart and a contrite spirit" (v. 7) can "answer the ends of the law" (v. 7). The atonement does not suspend the law; it satisfies what the law was for. Justice is answered, never overruled: the distinction powers every later atonement sermon in the record.

phrases.text: The record's formula for how anyone reaches God's presence: "no flesh that can dwell in the presence of God, save it be through the merits, and mercy, and grace of the Holy Messiah" (v. 8). Merits are his, not ours; the triple is deliberate and exclusive, and 2 Nephi 31 and Moroni will still be conjugating it at the record's far end.

phrases.text: The chapter's coinage and the record's ground rule: "it must needs be, that there is an opposition in all things" (v. 11). Not a regrettable condition but a structural one; righteousness, happiness, even existence require a contrary to be actual. The doctrine reframes every hardship the family has logged since Jerusalem: the record's afflictions belong to the structure.

phrases.term: Adam fell that men might be; and men are, that they might have joy
phrases.text: Fourteen words that reverse a millennium of mourning over Eden. The fall is read as descent with a destination, and the destination is named: being, then joy. The record's whole account of God's purposes compresses into the verse's second clause, and no later writer improves on it.

phrases.term: Free to choose liberty and eternal life
phrases.text: Freedom's full statement, with its price tag visible: men are free "according to the flesh" (v. 27) because the Mediator redeemed them into it, and the choice is between packaged destinies, liberty-and-life "through the great Mediator" (v. 27) or captivity-and-death under one "that all men might be miserable like unto himself" (v. 27). The chapter refuses any smaller menu.

verses.label: v. 1–4
verses.title: A blessing whose ground is the recipient's suffering
verses.text: The record opens the address by naming a hardship, not a virtue: "Thou art my firstborn in the days of my tribulation in the wilderness. And behold, in thy childhood thou hast suffered afflictions and much sorrow, because of the rudeness of thy brethren." What follows turns that into the promise: "he shall consecrate thine afflictions for thy gain." Verse 4 adds the other qualification, that he had already seen the glory of God in youth. Both credentials are things that happened to him rather than things he did.

verses.label: v. 14
verses.title: One distinction the rest of the chapter rests on
verses.text: In the middle of an argument the record introduces a category split in eight words: God "created all things, both the heavens and the earth, and all things that in them are, both things to act and things to be acted upon." Acting and being acted upon is the difference verse 13 has just used to reduce the denial to nothing, and it is the difference verse 16 will use for the freedom of the will. The clause is stated once, without illustration, and everything after it is built on it.

verses.label: v. 17
verses.title: An inference marked twice in one clause
verses.text: The record has the speaker flag his own reasoning and its source in the same breath: "I, Lehi, according to the things which I have read, must needs suppose that an angel of God, according to that which is written, had fallen from heaven." Two hedges surround the claim, one naming a document and one naming the act of inference. Must needs suppose stands in two verses of the volume, this one and Alma 46:41, and both times a writer is flagging a conclusion rather than reporting a revelation.

verses.label: v. 22–23
verses.title: A past that did not happen, worked out in full
verses.text: The record runs the alternative history instead of asserting the actual one: "if Adam had not transgressed he would not have fallen, but he would have remained in the garden of Eden. And all things which were created must have remained in the same state in which they were after they were created." Verse 23 draws out the consequences one at a time, no children, "a state of innocence, having no joy, for they knew no misery; doing no good, for they knew no sin." Four absences are listed, and each is paired with the knowledge that would have made it otherwise.

verses.label: v. 25
verses.title: Fourteen words, in two matched halves
verses.text: The chapter's argument closes on its shortest sentence: "Adam fell that men might be; and men are, that they might have joy." It ties with verse 20 for the briefest verse in the chapter. The two clauses share a structure, each with a subject, a verb, and a purpose, and the second takes its subject from the end of the first. Nothing is proved here. The verse states as a result what the previous fourteen verses argued for.

verses.label: v. 27–29
verses.title: Two options, each named with an agent attached
verses.text: The record puts the choice as two routes with two guides: "they are free to choose liberty and eternal life, through the great Mediator of all men, or to choose captivity and death, according to the captivity and power of the devil." Verse 28 states one side as an instruction, "look to the great Mediator, and hearken unto his great commandments," and verse 29 states the other as a prohibition, "not choose eternal death, according to the will of the flesh and the evil which is therein." Both are offered as choices, and both are said to place the chooser under someone.

chapter.title: A summit placed in a lap
chapter.text: The chapter is a blessing before it is a treatise, and it opens by naming the hearer's history: "in thy childhood thou hast suffered afflictions and much sorrow, because of the rudeness of thy brethren." Verse 2 states the intended use, "he shall consecrate thine afflictions for thy gain." The phrase "my firstborn in the wilderness" recurs at verse 11, in the middle of the argument about opposition, so the address to one son is kept inside the doctrine rather than dropped once the exposition begins.

chapter.title: Free salvation, real law
chapter.text: The chapter holds both poles without blinking: no flesh justified by law, and the law's ends still answered, never waived. Grace in Lehi's teaching is not law's defeat but law's satisfaction. That lets the record preach mercy for a thousand years without going soft on justice.

chapter.title: Opposition is architecture
chapter.text: Contraries are the world's working design: no bitter, no sweet; no misery, no joy; no alternative, no act. The doctrine gives the record its standing answer to every why-affliction question it will ever raise, beginning with Jacob's own.

chapter.title: Agency is engineered
chapter.text: Three conditions, all supplied: sufficient instruction, a law in force, and enticement from both sides. Freedom in this chapter is a built condition God maintains, at cost, including the cost of a permitted tempter.

chapter.title: The cheerful fall
chapter.text: Where exile readings mourn Eden, Lehi audits it: no fall, no family, no joy, no purpose. Verse 25 is the boldest revaluation in scripture, and the record earns it by the same logic that consecrates Jacob's afflictions: descent with a Redeemer attached is a route.

chapter.title: Freedom is purchased, then exercised
chapter.text: Verse 26 puts the order beyond doubt with a causal clause: "because that they are redeemed from the fall they have become free forever... to act for themselves and not to be acted upon." Verse 16 has already ruled out a neutral condition, "man could not act for himself save it should be that he was enticed by the one or the other." Verse 27 then names the two options and attaches each to a person, liberty and eternal life "through the great Mediator of all men," captivity and death "according to the captivity and power of the devil." The capacity to choose is presented as itself a gift from one of the two parties being chosen between.

chapter.title: The sermon Jacob will preach forever
chapter.text: Broken heart, answered law, merits and mercy and grace, firstfruits: Jacob's own great discourses (2 Ne. 9; Jacob 4) are this chapter expanded. Lehi's blessing turns out to be a commissioning; the wounded son becomes the family's theologian of the Redeemer.

applications.title: Ask for the consecration
applications.text: Take your oldest affliction and pray Lehi's grammar over it: not only "take this away" but "employ this for my gain." Then watch for the employment; consecrated wounds tend to become credentials for someone else's rescue.

applications.title: Bring the fee the law names
applications.text: The sacrifice answers the law only for the broken-hearted and contrite. Before the next sacrament, do the audit that produces those two things honestly: one specific sin grieved, one specific softness offered. The atonement's reach is universal; its terms are exact.

applications.title: Thank God for the other enticement
applications.text: When temptation is loud, remember the doctrine: a pull in one direction only would end your agency. Treat the contrary pull as evidence the system is working, then use the freedom it proves you have.

applications.title: Run the vanishing test
applications.text: When some hardship tempts you to wish opposition away, follow Lehi's chain to its end: no contraries, no purpose, no you. The exercise does not shrink the hardship; it relocates it inside a world worth having.

applications.title: Read your Eden forward
applications.text: Identify the fall in your own story, the decision or loss that ended an innocence, and write what became possible only after it. Joy in this doctrine is downstream of departure; mourning the garden forever is refusing the point of leaving it.

applications.title: State the decision in full
applications.text: Once this week, take an actual decision you are drifting through and say both of its real destinations out loud, the verse's two and only two. Most drifting happens in decisions never stated plainly enough to be chosen.

questions.text: Which of my afflictions have I only asked God to end, never to use?
When did I last come to the sacrifice with an actually broken heart, and what breaks it?
Where am I treating a structural opposition in my life as a malfunction to escape rather than a condition to act in?
Which enticement do I pretend I do not feel, and what does denying it cost my honesty?
Do I believe the purpose of my existence is joy, and what in my daily conduct would suggest otherwise?
If I named my one object in my family's hearing, as Lehi did, what would it truthfully be?
